questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Nutrient transfer in a mycorrhizal plant
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a mycorrhizal fungus supplies a plant with minerals and water
questions.stem: A chef's costing sheet notes that the wild mushrooms served with his roots come from plants growing beside oak trees, and he asks why.

options.text: The fungus breaks down leaf litter in the soil and releases the minerals for the plant roots to take up
options.misconception: thinks the fungus only decomposes litter and feeds the plant

options.text: The fungal hyphae reach beyond the root hairs and supply phosphate and water the plant could not reach
The mushroom cap releases sugars into the tree roots in exchange for the tree's shelter and shade
options.misconception: reverses the exchange and makes the tree the sugar source

options.text: The plant feeds sugars to the fungus, which converts them into phosphate that the fine roots then absorb
options.misconception: believes the fungus manufactures phosphate from sugar

questions.explanation: A mycorrhizal fungus trades minerals and water for plant sugars, and its hyphae extend the root's absorptive reach. Treating it as a litter decomposer that just fertilises the plant misses the two-way partnership.
questions.hint: Think about which partner supplies the scarce mineral.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the two partners that make up a lichen thallus
questions.stem: A chef's tasting notes record that a grey-green crust on the headland rock is sold as lichen, and the buyer wants to know what the thallus contains.

options.text: A single species of fungus with photosynthetic cells growing inside its own hyphae
options.misconception: treats the thallus as one hybrid organism

options.text: A fungus carrying green algal cells in its tissues without any bacterial partner
options.misconception: assumes a bacterial partner is always present

options.text: An alga that has invaded the hyphae of a fungal host and now feeds on it
options.misconception: makes the alga the parasite rather than the partner

options.text: A fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually an alga or cyanobacterium, living in a stable association

questions.explanation: A lichen thallus is a symbiosis between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner supplying sugars. Option A wrongly merges the two into one species, and option C turns the mutualism into parasitism.
questions.hint: Name both organisms before naming the structure.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a lichen thallus gains and holds water
questions.stem: A chef's delivery is delayed by rain, and he wonders why the lichen on his supplier's wall looks swollen and darker after a wet night.

options.text: Lichen hyphae absorb liquid water directly across their surfaces, swelling as it fills spaces within the thallus
Lichen thalli draw water from a vascular bundle that runs through the middle of the thallus
options.misconception: assumes lichens have vascular tissue like a plant

options.text: The algal partner pumps water upward from the rock, and the fungus stores it in its hyphal walls
options.misconception: gives the alga a pumping and storage role it does not have

options.text: Lichens avoid water loss by growing only on dry faces, so the dark colour comes from dust and soot
options.misconception: claims lichens are hydrophobic and never wet

questions.explanation: Lichens lack vascular tissue and take up water across the whole thallus surface, so they darken and swell in wet conditions. Option B invents a vascular bundle, and option D contradicts the visible swelling after rain.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe the reproductive function of a mushroom cap
questions.stem: A chef's costing sheet describes a cap that swells in the dark and releases a dusty puff when the box is opened. Explain what the cap is for.

answer.exemplar: The cap is the basidiomycete fruiting body, a reproductive structure that raises the spore-bearing gill surface into the moving air so spores disperse. The dusty puff is the release of millions of basidiospores, and the swelling in the dark is a response to moisture rather than to light.

questions.explanation: Fruiting bodies exist to disperse spores, and the cap raises the gill surface where basidiospores are formed into the airflow. Describing the cap as a feeding or growing organ misses its reproductive role.
questions.hint: Ask what structure is built to release spores.

options.misconception: assigns a zygomycete sporangium to a cup fungus

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a lichen survives drying and rehydrates
questions.stem: A chef's supplier explains that a lichen thallus swells after rain and shrivels in dry wind. Explain how the thallus handles water.

answer.exemplar: The thallus absorbs liquid water directly across its surfaces, through the cortex and algal layer, and holds it in the spaces between the fungal hyphae. The fungus also has hydrophilic cell walls that hold water and gel when it rains, which is why wet lichens darken and swell, and why they dry back to a grey brittle state when the water evaporates.

questions.explanation: Lichens take up liquid water over the whole thallus surface and hold it around the hyphae, so they swell and darken when wet. Describing a root and stem supply invents structures the lichen does not have.
questions.hint: Consider the surface area available for soaking.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Nutrient transfer in a mycorrhizal plant
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a mycorrhizal plant gains minerals from poor soil
questions.stem: A chef's supplier notes that a mycorrhizal plant grows well in poor soil. Explain how the plant gains minerals from the fungus.

answer.exemplar: The fungus grows outward from the root as a network of hyphae, which thread between soil particles into pores the root hairs cannot reach. The hyphae absorb phosphate, nitrate and water, pass them into the root cells, and the plant returns sugar made by photosynthesis. The extra reach of the hyphae is what lets the plant exploit poor soil.

questions.explanation: Hyphae explore far more soil than root hairs, absorb scarce ions such as phosphate, and pass them into the root for sugars. Describing the fungus as merely decomposing litter misses the mineral transfer.
questions.hint: Think about the reach of a hyphal thread.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare the role of yeast in bread making and in savoury glazes
questions.stem: A chef uses a yeast starter for both bread and a savoury glaze. Explain what the yeast is doing in each case.

answer.exemplar: In the bread the yeast ferments sugars in the flour, and the carbon dioxide it releases is trapped by the gluten so the dough rises, while the ethanol and other compounds are driven off in the bake. In the savoury glaze the same yeast converts sugars on the surface of the food into carbon dioxide and ethanol, and the browning and savoury aroma come from Maillard reactions and from the alcohol evaporating.

questions.explanation: Both uses ferment sugars, but the useful product differs: trapped gas raises bread, while alcohol and flavour compounds season a glaze. Saying the yeast breaks down gluten mistakes its role.
questions.hint: Same organism, different product that matters.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment testing the partnership nature of a lichen
questions.stem: A chef's lab wants to show that a lichen is a partnership rather than one unusual fungus. Design a comparison that would support this.

answer.exemplar: Sample the same lichen thallus, then separate the material into fungal hyphae and the green algal partner, for example by gentle crushing and sieving under a microscope. Prepare a treatment with the fungus and alga together and a control with the fungus alone, grown in matched flasks with the same light, nutrients and water. If the fungus alone grows poorly or makes no thallus while the combined culture forms a thallus, that supports the partnership claim.

questions.explanation: To test a partnership you separate the partners and test them apart and together under matched conditions. Only a combined culture that forms a thallus supports the claim, so the fungus alone is not enough.
questions.hint: Include controls and a together treatment.

answer.exemplar: Set up identical agar plates inoculated with the same amount of a fresh culture and incubate them at a series of temperatures, for example 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 degrees, keeping the light, medium and time constant. questions.learningObjective: Design a test for whether freezing kills a culture
questions.stem: A chef's lab suspects its freezer is killing a starter culture. Design a test that would show whether freezing is the cause.

answer.exemplar: Take one culture of the same age and split it into matched portions. If only the frozen portion fails to grow while the chilled and warm portions do, freezing is implicated, and the chilled control also separates chill damage from freeze damage.

questions.explanation: Lichens tolerate salt and desiccation together, so splash-zone specimens survive where a leafy plant would lose water and take up damaging salt. Option D wrongly claims the thallus has no cells, and option A invents a waterproof skin.
questions.hint: Combine salt tolerance with water loss.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total spores collected across many traps
questions.stem: A chef's field survey uses 250 spore traps, each collecting 120 spores over a week. How many spores were collected in total?
questions.explanation: Two hundred and fifty traps at 120 spores each give 250 times 120, which is 30000 spores. An answer of 370 adds rather than multiplies, and 3000 misses a factor of ten.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of traps by the spores per trap.
